p: Priya counted twenty three ask Anders notes in the margins of her old runbook, and wrote down eleven rules that lived only in people's heads.
The rules went into a Copilot instructions file in Lumen, reviewed like code, and Anders's Terraform rules got a file of their own.
Kraków got a shared prompt for date tests. Renata learned to give Copilot invented examples after Ken's scanner caught real looking rows she'd pasted from staging.
Anders approved the house rules after they planted the old bug in a test pull request and watched Copilot catch it.
At Sunday dinner Priya wrote her grandmother's dal on one of Asha's index cards, with both sides of the jaggery argument on it.
Then Ken asked for Monday morning. He wanted to talk about staging.
Ken Ito. Security lead. When he says staging, he's already found something.
Nora Kim. Compliance. She'll ask the same question twice if it matters.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. The board meets Thursday at ten.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. Her fixtures prompt is the one the scanner flagged.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Slower than he used to be, on purpose.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. His Terraform rules finally live in a file.
Monday came on time for once. Priya was up at six because she'd set an alarm for six, and her phone already had Ken's invite for eight o'clock. Staging. No description. Ken never wrote descriptions.

Asha's cards came at 6:40, five photos, purple felt tip. Across the top card: Week six. Fences. Every ER I worked in had locked doors and curtains. The trick was knowing which one you were standing behind.
At 7:05 a message came in from Tomasz in Kraków. Ken's invite says staging. Should I worry for my team, or for me? She didn't know yet, so she told him that.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: Thursday. The board is Thursday at ten. Elena will ask about the date bug. If there's anything else I should know before then, I'd like to hear it from you before I hear it from a board member. Joyce
She drove in with Ken's Friday message still in her head. The scanner sees pull requests. It never saw what went to Copilot before one was opened.
Asha's first card said: A curtain gives a patient privacy from the hallway. It doesn't stop the next bed from hearing. Know which one you've got.

Under it Priya wrote what the GitHub docs say. Content exclusion, a Business and Enterprise feature, tells Copilot to ignore chosen files: no inline suggestions there, no use of their content in suggestions elsewhere or in answers, and no code review. A repository administrator's rules cover any Copilot user in the enterprise working in that repository. An organization owner's rules cover people who get their seat from that organization. An enterprise owner's cover every Copilot user in the enterprise. A personal plan sits outside all of them.

Rules are paths, one per line, in fnmatch patterns that ignore case. Organization rules name the repository first, or for every repository and files outside Git. "/scripts/*" matches files directly in that folder; "/scripts/**" matches everything in or below it. Limits: exclusion isn't supported in the Edit and Agent modes of Copilot Chat in VS Code. GitHub's note says other editors too, though its table now marks chat and agent supported in Visual Studio and JetBrains IDEs, so test before you trust it. It doesn't apply to symbolic links or repositories on remote filesystems. The IDE can still pass along semantic information from an excluded file, like types and hover definitions. On GitHub.com it's in public preview. In your own VS Code, the github.copilot.enable setting turns Copilot off by language, such as "markdown": false. An exclusion keeps data out of context. It doesn't make data safe that shouldn't exist.
How the exam asks it. Know who can set exclusions and whom each level covers, the path format, and the limits: agent and edit modes, symlinks, remote filesystems, and what the IDE passes along.
Lock it, then try the handle.
The second card: Locking the drug room door was half the job. A good charge nurse tried the handle on the way past.

A changed exclusion can take up to 30 minutes to reach an IDE that already loaded the settings. In VS Code, run Developer: Reload Window from the Command Palette instead of waiting. In Visual Studio and JetBrains IDEs, restart the application. Vim and Neovim fetch exclusions each time a file opens. In an excluded file, the Copilot status bar icon has a diagonal line through it, and its tooltip names the settings that applied.

Then test it as the docs describe. Make an edit in a file that isn't excluded, to prove Copilot is working. Make the same edit in an excluded file and expect nothing. For chat, attach only the excluded file and ask Copilot to explain it. It shouldn't be able to, and the file shouldn't appear in References. When exclusions "don't work," check the timing, then whether the pattern matches, a symlink or remote filesystem, agent mode, and whose seat it is. The settings page shows who last changed the rules and when, and owners can manage exclusions through the REST API.
How the exam asks it. If exclusions seem not to work, think timing first: up to 30 minutes, or reload. Then the pattern, the surface, and whose seat it is.
The third card: When a family gives you the history, write down who said it. It matters later.

In under one percent of suggestions, by GitHub's count, what Copilot predicts matches public code. The Suggestions matching public code policy decides what happens. On Block, Copilot checks a suggestion plus about 150 characters around it against an index of public GitHub code and doesn't show a match or near match. On Allow, it appears, and code referencing shows where similar code lives and its license. In VS Code, accepted matches are logged in the Output panel under GitHub Copilot Log (Code References). In chat, a response with matching code links to the matches.

For people with a Business or Enterprise seat, the organization's policy applies, not a personal setting, and between two organizations the more restrictive wins. That's a privacy policy rule. Most features go the other way: if any of a person's organizations turns a feature on, they get it. The cloud agent and Copilot CLI can still produce matching code with Block set; the cloud agent shows matches in its session logs. On ownership, GitHub doesn't claim ownership of suggestions. Whether one can be owned depends on things like local law. What you ship, and its licenses, are yours to check.
How the exam asks it. Block hides matches, checked with about 150 characters of context. Allow shows them with references and licenses. GitHub doesn't claim ownership of suggestions.
The fourth card: Anything you said at the nurses' station, somebody heard. Know who, and how long they'll remember.

Copilot builds a prompt from what you typed plus context: the open file, code near the cursor or selected, open tabs, instructions files, and chat history. Exclusion works at that first step. The editor fetches the policy by sending the repository's URL, which GitHub says isn't logged, and leaves excluded files out of context. The prompt goes over HTTPS to a proxy in a GitHub owned Azure tenant, filters screen it for manipulation, harmful content, and personal data, and the model answers. Post processing filters the answer, checks for common bugs and vulnerabilities, and applies Block if it's set.

Retention depends on the surface. GitHub's Copilot FAQ gives these Business and Enterprise defaults: prompts and suggestions from IDE chat and code completions aren't retained. On GitHub.com, mobile, and the CLI, they're kept 28 days. User engagement data is kept two years. Business and Enterprise data doesn't train GitHub's models. Anyone with access to the repository can read cloud agent session logs on GitHub.com. Not retained doesn't mean not sent, which is why privacy and security, one of the six responsible AI principles, starts with keeping sensitive data out of context.

How the exam asks it. IDE chat and completions on Business or Enterprise: not retained. GitHub.com, mobile, and CLI: 28 days. No training on Business or Enterprise data. Exclusions act when context is gathered.
Chart it, or it didn't happen.
The last card: We said it a hundred times a night. If you didn't chart it, you didn't do it.

The organization audit log holds Copilot's settings history. Search action:copilot. copilot.content_exclusion_changed records a change to excluded paths, with the saved rules in its details. copilot.cfb_seat_added records a seat granted, copilot.cfb_org_settings_changed a feature settings change, and copilot.code_review_organization_settings_updated a code review settings change. In an enterprise log, actor:Copilot shows agent activity. Events last 180 days, so export or stream them for longer evidence. Prompts people type in their editors aren't in the log.

A user follows the policies of whoever gives them a Business or Enterprise seat, enterprise policy beats organization policy, and an individual plan is cancelled when its owner joins Business or Enterprise. Not every policy reaches every surface, and GitHub keeps a table. The content exclusion policy doesn't reach third party agents or Spark. It does reach the cloud agent, in public preview, which is the agent on GitHub.com, not agent mode in your editor. The public code policy covers IDEs, and agents in annotate mode only, but not Chat on GitHub.com, the CLI, or code review. Code review can be requested automatically through a ruleset.
How the exam asks it. Know action:copilot, the content exclusion event, 180 days, and no prompts. Know enterprise beats organization, and that a policy can skip some surfaces.
Ken had printed pages for the eight o'clock, which nobody at Halcyon did anymore. He handed one each to Priya, Nora, Joyce, and Renata. Renata took hers like it might be a summons.

Ken's page. The staging seed folder in lumen forecast, under fixtures, holds fourteen tables, and two of them, pre admissions and contacts, never went through the scrub script, which is older than both. On Thursday two pre admissions rows turned up in a prompt file with real looking dates of birth, and since he can't prove they're real, he's treating them as real. On Friday the pre admissions file was listed under References in two engineers' recent Copilot Chat threads, and no content exclusion covers the folder.

Some of Lumen was always going to sit close to patients, Ken said. The hospital files under config are unit names, bed counts, discharge rules. Cascade Valley Health's has forty units in it. That's why my October list exists. This folder was never on it, because nobody thought forecast had data in it.

Priya read the path twice. She knew it. Step fourteen of her July migration runbook: copy the staging seed into lumen-forecast/fixtures, already scrubbed. She'd written already scrubbed because the old README said so.
That folder came over in my migration, she said. Step fourteen. I copied it, and I didn't check it.
Across the table Renata put her page down flat. It was the first time since Ken handed it to her that she'd let go of it.
Ken had known. He'd waited for her to say it. Then what do we do today?
Answer. Add a rule to the instructions file and tell Copilot to skip that folder.
B. Ask everyone to close the seed files and keep them out of Copilot chats.
C. Exclude the seed folder from Copilot today, then scrub the real rows.
D. Exclude the whole lumen-forecast repository until every table is scrubbed.

Ken adds the folder to the organization's exclusions after lunch, and the scrub goes on his list for the week, Renata's prompt file included. Nora writes two lines in her log: exclusion added Monday, scrub in progress. The rule keeps it out of Copilot. It doesn't make the rows go away. Renata writes today, then scrub at the top of her page and underlines it.

That's the move. Content exclusion keeps chosen files from being used as context on Business and Enterprise, so it's the fast control. It doesn't clean data that shouldn't be there. Pair it with removing the real records.
Decision two. One star or two.
At one Ken sent her the change before he saved it. He wanted a second reader, he said, because he'd been the only reader on the October list.

Ken's draft of the organization content exclusion. The October list stays above it, unchanged. Under it is one new entry for the lumen forecast repository: slash fixtures, slash staging seed, slash, and then a single star.
The seed folder had a contacts file at the top and a subfolder for each year since 2023. pre_admissions.csv lived in two of the year folders.
Answer. Replace it with a *.csv pattern that catches every seed file in the repo.
B. Yes, one star after the folder covers everything inside it at any depth.
C. Change the line to /fixtures/staging-seed/** with two stars at the end.
D. Keep that line and add one more for each year's subfolder under it.

Ken adds the second star, reads the line under his breath, and saves it at 1:20. One star, the folder. Two, everything under it. His name and the time show up at the bottom of the settings page. Priya asks him to leave the October list exactly as it is, comments and all. He'd already planned to.

Good. That's the call. The paths are fnmatch patterns, and case doesn't matter. One star gets you the files sitting in that folder. Two gets every file in it or under it. At the organization level you write the repository's name, then its paths beneath.
At 1:35 Devin sent her a screen recording, forty seconds long.

In it he opened fixtures/staging-seed/contacts.csv to start on Ken's scrub list, typed a comma at the end of a row, and gray text filled in the rest of it. That's somebody's phone number shape, he said in the recording, quieter.
In the corner of the recording, the yellow page that said Careful was still taped under his monitor.
Ken had saved the rule fifteen minutes earlier. Devin's VS Code had been open since eight.
Ken's rule is in. This file still gets suggestions. Is the fence broken, or is it me? I'm asking before I decide.
Devin's editor, open since eight, still completes rows in a CSV Ken excluded at 1:20. What should he do?
Answer. Reinstall the Copilot extension to clear whatever old rules it cached.
B. Reload his VS Code window and check the Copilot icon on that file.
C. Have Ken delete the rule, save it again and push it out to editors.
D. Wait half an hour for the change to reach his editor and try again.

He runs Developer: Reload Window from the Command Palette. When the window comes back, the Copilot icon in the status bar has a line through it, and the tooltip names Halcyon's organization settings. The gray text is gone. So it wasn't broken. It just hadn't heard yet. He types the next row of the scrub list by hand.

Exactly right. After a content exclusion changes, an IDE that already loaded the settings can take up to 30 minutes to pick it up. In VS Code, Developer: Reload Window applies it now. In an excluded file the Copilot icon shows a diagonal line, and its tooltip says which settings applied.
Tuesday morning Renata posted a question in the rollout channel. Nobody answered it. Six people reacted with the eyes emoji, which wasn't an answer either.
At eleven she came to Priya's desk with her laptop open. I said it in the channel. I'm saying it again here.
The second time, Priya thought. She stopped typing.

Renata had been writing a test in calculateWindow.test.ts, which nobody had excluded. Copilot had suggested a fixture with a field called preAdmitSurgeryTime. That name existed in one place in the repository: a types file in the seed folder.
The folder's excluded. So how does it know the name?
Answer. Treat it as the known IDE limit and get the real data out of those files.
B. Rename the fields in the types file to names that give nothing away.
C. Report it to GitHub as a bug and pause Copilot in lumen-forecast meanwhile.
D. Exclude every file in the repo that imports types from the seed folder.

They read the limitation together. The IDE can hand Copilot semantic details from an excluded file, like types and hover definitions. A field name isn't a patient. A row is. The rule narrows what goes out. Getting the real rows out is what makes it safe. Renata writes that down, then looks up. Nobody answered me in the channel. I know. You came anyway.

That's the move. The IDE can hand Copilot details from an excluded file on its own, like types, hover definitions, and build settings. That's a documented limit. Exclusion reduces exposure. Removing the sensitive data closes it.
Decision five. Agent in the folder.
Wednesday at 7:10 Tomasz called with his camera on. It was after three in the afternoon in Kraków, and his coffee had gone cold beside him.

One of my engineers used agent mode in VS Code yesterday to move our fixtures to the new shape. All of them. It changed eleven files in the seed folder, the year folders too. Ken's scanner flagged the pull request an hour ago. The folder is excluded. How did the agent get in?

Ken's guide had said since October: no agent mode in excluded repositories. Everyone had read that as the hospital config. The seed folder had only been excluded since Monday, and nobody had told Kraków the line reached it now.
Agent mode changed eleven files inside the excluded seed folder. What should Priya tell Tomasz?
Answer. Explain that agent mode ignores exclusions and keep it out of the folder.
B. Have the engineer close the seed files before starting an agent session.
C. Add the folder again at the enterprise level and make agent mode honor it.
D. Move the seed into its own repository and exclude that repository whole.

Exclusions don't apply to agent mode or edit mode in VS Code. It isn't a setting. It's a documented limit. Tomasz closes the pull request himself and posts the rule in Polish and English: no agent mode on excluded paths until the seed is clean. Ken adds the same line to the guide and dates it. So the fence is for some of Copilot. For now. We read the list again when the docs change.

Good. That's the call. Content exclusion isn't supported in the Edit and Agent modes of Copilot Chat in VS Code. When a control has a known gap, cover it with another one, like keeping agents off those paths, and recheck the docs as support changes.
Decision six. Where the rows went.
Nora came by at ten with the question she'd been writing down since Monday.

Those rows went to Copilot at least three times that we know of. Renata's prompt in VS Code last Thursday. A chat on GitHub.com about the census job, with pre_admissions.csv in the references. And yesterday, agent mode in Kraków. Where are the rows now? Did GitHub keep them? Did it train on them? I want to write it down right the first time.
The rows reached Copilot in an editor, on the web and through an agent. What should Nora be told?
Answer. All of it is kept for 28 days and may be used to train GitHub's models.
B. Business data is never used for training, and beyond that we can't know.
C. Nothing was kept anywhere: Copilot drops every prompt once it answers.
D. VS Code prompts weren't kept, the GitHub.com chat lasts 28 days, no training.

Priya pulls up GitHub's Copilot FAQ and reads the defaults with her. On Business, prompts and suggestions from IDE chat and completions aren't retained. On GitHub.com, mobile, and the CLI they're kept for 28 days. Engagement data stays two years. None of it trains GitHub's models. Nora writes it in two columns, then adds a line under both. Not kept doesn't mean not sent. No. They were sent. That's why the rows are coming out.

Exactly right. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, GitHub's defaults are: IDE chat and code completions, prompts and suggestions not retained; Copilot on GitHub.com, mobile, and the CLI, kept 28 days; engagement data two years. Business and Enterprise data isn't used for training. Personal plans are different: GitHub may train on them unless the user opts out.
Decision seven. Something that isn't Ken.
At two Nora was back with a different question and the same notebook.
The auditors will ask when the seed folder was excluded, who did it, and what the rule said that day. Not what it says now. Ken says he saved it Monday. I need something that isn't Ken saying so.
Ken, across the table, didn't look offended. I'd want that too.
Nora needs proof of when the seed exclusion was saved and what it said. What evidence should Priya give?
Answer. Screenshot the content exclusion settings page, with the date in the corner.
B. Have Ken write and sign a memo with the date and the exact text of the rule.
C. Filter the audit log for copilot.content_exclusion_changed and export it.
D. Pull Copilot's usage metrics showing when the folder stopped being used.

From the bottom of the Copilot settings page, Ken clicks the time of his last change and lands in the organization audit log, filtered to the event for content exclusion changes. Monday, his name, and in the details the excluded paths exactly as saved. They export the week to Nora's evidence folder, since the log keeps 180 days. And what people typed? Not in there. Never was. Nora had asked in October. She'd wanted to hear it the same way twice.

That's the move. The audit log records Copilot settings changes. copilot.content_exclusion_changed shows who changed excluded paths and when, with the saved rules in its details, and the settings page links straight to it. Events are kept for 180 days, and prompts aren't included.
Thursday at 7:40 Joyce sent her the board slide with one line highlighted.
Board slide 6, draft. Since the incident: Copilot's house rules live in the Lumen repositories, reviewed like code. Copilot can no longer see patient data anywhere at Halcyon.

Under it Joyce had written: The second sentence is the one they'll remember. Is it true? I told a board can't once, my first year as a CTO, about backups. I spent the next year taking it back. I'd rather not do that at ten this morning.

Priya read the sentence again. The true version had a folder in it, and the folder had come over on her plan. Joyce knew that. She'd been in the room Monday when Priya said it, and she was asking anyway.
Joyce's board slide claims Copilot can no longer see patient data anywhere. How should the sentence change?
Answer. Leave it as it is now that the folder is excluded and the rows are going.
B. Rewrite it to name what's excluded and where exclusions don't reach.
C. Cut the Copilot sentence from the slide and keep to the date bug.
D. Change can't to shouldn't and leave the rest of the sentence alone.

They rewrite it together. The seed folder joins the October list, excluded for everyone with a Halcyon seat. Agent mode and some other surfaces don't honor exclusions, so agents stay off those paths. The real rows are being removed this week. Joyce reads it more slowly than she reads most things. It's longer. It's still true on Friday. Good. That's twice this week you told me before anybody else could.

Good. That's the call. Policies and exclusions apply on some surfaces and not others, and only to people who get Copilot from the organization. GitHub publishes which policies reach which surfaces. An honest claim names the control, its limits, and what covers the gap.
The board ended at noon. Joyce's message was one line: They asked about agent mode. It was already on the slide.
At three Anders pulled a chair up to her desk without asking.
He was writing a backup bucket module for staging, the kind of Terraform half the internet has written. Every other line filled in fine. The part he wanted never appeared.
His Terraform instructions file was open in the next tab. He'd added two rules to it since Friday.
I read the docs before I came over. Ken set the public code filter to block in October. That's what's eating it. My team wants it on allow. I said I'd ask you, because Ken would say no in one word.
The org's public code setting hides a common piece of Terraform Anders needs. What should Priya decide?
Answer. Switch the org policy to Allow for now and unblock the infra team.
B. Have each engineer on the team switch to Allow in their own settings.
C. Set Allow and have the team read the code references log before accepting.
D. Keep Block on for the org and write that block from the provider's docs.

Block isn't saying the code's wrong. It's saying it matches something public, checked with about a hundred and fifty characters around it, and we can't see whose or under what license. Anders thinks about that. Then he writes the block himself in twenty minutes from the provider's docs and asks Copilot Chat to check it against them. It finds a missing tag. Fine. That's useful. He says it like it costs him something, and he says it anyway.

Exactly right. With Block, Copilot checks suggestions plus about 150 characters of surrounding code against public code on GitHub and doesn't show matches. That guards against code with a license nobody chose. People with org seats get the org's setting.
Friday at nine Nora sent Priya a diagram for the auditors and asked her to mark it up before Ken saw it. He'll be kind about it. I'd rather be right.

Nora's draft, in five steps. Step one, the developer types in the editor, and step two, Copilot sends the prompt and the open files to GitHub. Step three, the proxy removes any excluded files from the prompt; step four, the model answers; and step five, filters check the answer, and the developer sees it.
Nora had circled step three herself, with a question mark next to it.
Nora's draft diagram shows how a Copilot request travels. How should Priya mark it up?
Answer. Cut step three: the model reads excluded files but is told to skip them.
B. Keep step three: the proxy is where excluded files get stripped out.
C. Keep step three and add that filters check answers for public code too.
D. Move exclusions to step two: the editor leaves those files out of context.

The editor asks GitHub for the policy first. It sends the repository's URL to ask, and GitHub says it doesn't log those. Then it builds the prompt without the excluded files. They redraw it: context gathered, minus exclusions. Prompt built. HTTPS to the proxy. Filters for manipulation, harmful content, and personal data. The model. Filters again, for content, code quality, and public code. Nora goes down it with her pen and doesn't circle anything.

That's the move. Content exclusion works on the context Copilot gathers, before the prompt is built. The client gets the policy for the repository and leaves excluded content out. The proxy and filters come after, on the way to the model and back.

At two Ken's scrub merged. pre_admissions and contacts were gone, replaced with rows for people who had never existed: invented names, invented dates, three date fields and a time zone in every row, in the shape Renata had worked out the week before.
Then he pulled the week's Copilot entries from the audit log, because he always did before he closed anything.

The organization audit log, Copilot entries this week, where every content exclusion change shows as copilot dot content exclusion changed. Ken made one on Monday at 1:20. On Friday at 1:58, Ken added a Copilot Business seat.
The last line was a new engineer in Kraków who started Monday. Ken had checked that too.
Before I tell Nora it's closed, how do we know the fence holds? I'm not signing a line I haven't tested.
Answer. Try a file that isn't excluded, then a seed file, then a Chat question.
B. Open a seed file and check that the Copilot icon has a line through it.
C. Trust the settings page: the rule is saved, dated, under Ken's name.
D. Ask Copilot Chat whether it can see anything in the seed folder right now.

They follow the docs step by step. In calculateWindow.ts an edit gets a suggestion, so Copilot is working. The same edit in a seed file gets nothing, and the icon has its line through it. With only the seed file open and attached, they ask Chat to explain this file. It can't, and the file isn't in the References. Ken writes the evidence line and leaves room under his name. You copied it in. You should sign that it's out. Priya signs. Then she opens the July runbook to step fourteen, crosses out already scrubbed, and writes: checked, November 13.

Good. That's the call. To test content exclusion, confirm Copilot works in a file that isn't excluded, then make the same edit in an excluded file and expect no suggestion. For chat, attach only the excluded file and ask about it. Copilot shouldn't use it, and it shouldn't be listed in References.
At 4:30 Nora's evidence log had a new line in it, tested and signed by two people.
The staging seed was scrubbed. Not mostly.
The public code filter stayed on Block. Anders's module merged at five with a comment on its first line: written, not suggested.
Most of what she'd learned this week was where the fences didn't reach. She'd rather know that on a Friday in November than hear it from an auditor in March.
On Saturday she drove to Asha's. Asha's back gate had sagged until it wouldn't latch, and Raj had come with a drill and an opinion.
Priya held the gate while he worked and told them about step fourteen: already scrubbed, because a README said so, on a plan with her name at the top.
And who said it was yours?
Me. Monday morning, before anybody asked. Asha nodded and didn't say good, which from her meant good.

Her father set the drill down. First job they gave me with my name on the ticket, I scrapped twenty two parts. Wrong offset. I'd copied it off the last man's sheet. Foreman made me fill out the scrap tags myself. All twenty two. Same capitals I'd put on the ticket.
I kept a tag. He didn't say where. Asha did. His wallet. Since 1979.
He shut the gate and the latch caught. Then he sent Priya around to the alley side. Push it like you want in.
She put her shoulder into it. It held.
Again, he said, and she pushed again, harder, and it held again, and Asha went in to put the kettle on.
